passage: The Class 4 room smelled of chalk and wet umbrellas. Ma'am pinned up a picture of the colony market and asked, "How many cycles are parked outside the sweet shop?" Vasudha counted. Five. She counted again, touching each one with her eyes. Five. "Four!" said Parul from the front bench, and her friends nodded. "Four, ma'am." Hands shot up for four, one after another. Last week, when Vasudha had said "Mars" instead of "Jupiter", the back row had giggled for the whole period. Her cheeks still remembered it. Slowly her hand went up with the rest. "Four," she mumbled. Ma'am turned the picture towards the window light. "Count again, everyone." Vasudha stared at the fifth cycle, half hidden behind a fruit cart, and wished her hand had stayed down.

qa.q: How many cycles did Vasudha count outside the sweet shop?
qa.a: Vasudha counted five cycles, and counted again to be sure.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha raise her hand for four even though she had counted five?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at again, because the back row had giggled the whole period when she said "Mars" last week.

qa.q: At the moment the hands went up, what choice could Vasudha have made instead?
qa.a: She could have said she counted five and pointed to the cycle behind the fruit cart, risking a few giggles but trusting her own eyes.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when ma'am asks everyone to count again?
qa.a: Parul might feel unsure and a little embarrassed, realising her quick answer made half the class copy it without checking.

grounding: A child copies the class's wrong answer although she can see the right one, because she fears being laughed at.

passage:
"Bhaiya, can I ask you something?" Aparna dropped her bag by the sofa.
"If it's quick. I've got tuition," Akash said.
"Today Sir asked which bean plant on the window was tallest. Everyone said the blue pot."
"So?"
"The red pot was taller. I could see it. It was touching the grill."
"Then why do you look like you lost a match?"
"Because I said blue too." She pulled at her sock. "Everyone was saying blue. If I said red alone, Kunal would call me Miss Red Pot for a month."
Akash sat down next to her. "Did Sir measure?"
"Tomorrow. With a scale."
"And if it's red?"
"Then I was right and I said the wrong thing." She groaned into a cushion. "Why did my mouth do that?"

qa.q: Which pot did Aparna see was taller?
qa.a: The red pot was taller; it was touching the grill.

qa.q: What was Aparna worried about when she said blue with everyone else?
qa.a: She worried that Kunal would call her Miss Red Pot for a month if she said red alone 😰

qa.q: When Sir measures tomorrow, what could Aparna choose to say?
qa.a: She could tell Sir she saw the red pot touching the grill and should have said so, a small way to stand by what she saw.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to see his sister's choice, judging from his questions?
qa.a: Akash doesn't scold; he sits beside her and asks whether Sir measured, as if helping her notice that the truth will come out anyway.

grounding: A child follows the class's answer though she can see it is wrong, because disagreeing alone risks being teased.

passage: Last year, in Class 3, our quiz team had to write one answer on the slate: how many legs does a spider have? I knew it was eight. I had counted them on the spider behind our bathroom door. But Kavitha said, "Six, obviously," and the other three said, "Yes, six." Then they all looked at me, because I was holding the chalk. My face got hot. If I said eight and was wrong, they would laugh the way they laughed when I read "island" as "is-land". So I wrote 6. We lost the point. On the way home I told Kavitha, "I knew it was eight." Kavitha stopped walking. "Then why didn't you say, Shalini?" I didn't have an answer. I still think about that chalk.

qa.q: How many legs did Shalini know a spider has?
qa.a: Shalini knew it was eight, from counting the legs on the spider behind the bathroom door.

qa.q: What was Shalini afraid of when the team looked at the chalk?
qa.a: Shalini was afraid of being laughed at for saying eight, the way the class laughed at "is-land".

qa.q: Which moment was the real choice for Shalini, and what could Shalini have done there?
qa.a: The choice came with the chalk in hand; Shalini could have said, "I counted them, it's eight," before writing anything.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel on hearing "I knew it was eight" on the walk home?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel surprised and a bit let down that a point was lost when a teammate knew the answer all along.

grounding: A child writes the group's wrong answer despite knowing the truth, because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 3, Thursday. Written by Jaya Ma'am.

In today's quick-quiz I asked, "Which is heavier: one kilo of cotton or one kilo of iron?" Rohit shouted, "Iron!" and the whole row repeated it. Jasleen, eight, sat very still. I saw her whisper "same" to herself and start writing it on her slate. Then she looked around at everyone saying iron. She rubbed out "same" with her sleeve and wrote "iron". When a boy laughed at Manu for a wrong answer earlier, Jasleen had laughed too, and I think she remembered it. At break she came to my desk and asked quietly, "Ma'am, is it the same?" I said yes. She looked at her grey sleeve.

What I did next: from tomorrow, children will write answers on their slates privately before anyone speaks.

qa.q: What did Jasleen first write on her slate?
qa.a: She started writing 'same' on her slate.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen rub out her answer?
qa.a: She was worried about being laughed at for being the only one to disagree, since the whole row was saying iron and she had seen Manu laughed at.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new rule a good step?
qa.a: Writing answers privately before anyone speaks lets children like Jasleen keep their own answer without feeling the pressure of the group.

qa.q: How might Manu feel about quiz time after being laughed at earlier?
qa.a: Manu may feel nervous and embarrassed, and less willing to answer aloud, just as the laughter made Jasleen afraid to disagree.

grounding: An eight-year-old knows the right answer but switches to the group's wrong answer because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage:
Saturday

Scouts map day. We had to find the old well using the map and a compass. Joseph was holding the map and said, "The stream goes this way, towards the hill." Everyone said, "Yes, yes, hill." I looked at the compass. The needle said the stream was going the other way. I was nearly sure.

But Joseph is the patrol leader, and all five of them were already walking. If I said "wrong way" and I was wrong, they'd call me Compass Girl for the whole camp. So I walked behind them and didn't say anything.

We walked for twenty minutes and ended up at a cow shed. Then Joseph turned the map around and went red. We went back the way I thought.

Nobody knew I had known. I feel stupid for being right and quiet.

- Gurleen

qa.q: Where did the patrol end up after walking for twenty minutes?
qa.a: They ended up at a cow shed.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep quiet even though the compass showed the other way?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she spoke alone and was wrong, the others would tease her and call her Compass Girl for the whole camp.

qa.q: What could Gurleen try next time she is nearly sure the group is wrong?
qa.a: She could quietly show Joseph the compass and ask Joseph to check, which is less scary than announcing that everyone is wrong.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel on learning Gurleen had known the right way?
qa.a: Joseph might feel embarrassed but also wish she had spoken, since it would have saved the whole patrol twenty minutes.

grounding: A ten-year-old sees the compass contradict the group but follows everyone, worried about being laughed at if she disagrees alone.

passage: In Siddiq's Toronto classroom, Ms Reyes held up a card with three lines on it. "Which one matches this line?" she asked, pointing to a fourth. Siddiq, ten, could see it was C, clearly. But one by one, the kids in front said "B." Tuan said "B." Even Maya, the smartest girl, said "B." Siddiq's face went hot. Was he seeing wrong? He looked again: C. Now it was his turn, and twenty faces turned toward him. His mouth went dry. If he said C, they'd laugh. "B," he said quietly. Ms Reyes smiled and explained: everyone before him had been told to say B on purpose, as a lesson. The answer was C. Siddiq stared at his desk. He'd been right all along, and he'd still said B.

qa.q: Which line did Siddiq see was the match?
qa.a: He could see it was C, clearly.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq say "B" when he saw C?
qa.a: Siddiq felt anxious and exposed, afraid the class would laugh if he disagreed with everyone.

qa.q: What could Siddiq tell himself next time he sees something different from the group?
qa.a: Siddiq could remind himself that his eyes are evidence too, and that saying what he sees is worth a moment of awkwardness.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt saying "B" on purpose while watching Siddiq?
qa.a: Tuan might have felt a bit guilty or curious, watching Siddiq struggle with an answer everyone knew was wrong.

grounding: A child sees everyone pick the same wrong answer and follows the group even though the truth is visible, afraid of being laughed at.

passage: At the school science club in Madurai, the teacher placed two potted plants on the table. "Which one got more sunlight this week?" Lakshmi, nine, had watered them every day. She knew the left one had stood by the window. But Bhavna, the club captain, said, "Right one, obviously," and everyone agreed, nodding and giggling. "Lakshmi?" the teacher asked. Lakshmi's cheeks burned. The others were looking. She thought of the window, then of Bhavna rolling her eyes. "Right one," she mumbled. The teacher checked the logbook. "Actually, the left one. Lakshmi, you watered them. Didn't you notice?" A few children laughed after all. Lakshmi wanted to disappear. She'd been laughed at anyway, just for the wrong reason.

qa.q: Where had the left plant stood?
qa.a: The left one had stood by the window.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when the teacher asked her?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt embarrassed and anxious, her cheeks burning because disagreeing with Bhavna and the group felt risky.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Lakshmi try next time?
qa.a: Lakshmi hid what she knew to avoid being laughed at; next time she could say what she saw calmly, since her evidence was real.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when the logbook showed she was wrong?
qa.a: Bhavna may have felt embarrassed too, having led everyone to the wrong answer.

grounding: A child sees the group choose an answer she knows is wrong and follows it, afraid of being laughed at, even though the truth was visible.

passage:
Monday: In class five, the teacher wrote "recieve" on the board and asked if it was spelled right. Everyone shouted "Yes!" Bhupen, ten, was sure it was "ei," but Zubin next to him shouted "Yes!" too. Bhupen said "yes," quietly.
Wednesday: In the spelling test, Bhupen wrote "receive," the way he'd always known. He felt a knot of worry. What if they were all right and he was wrong?
Friday: Marks came back. Bhupen got it right. The teacher said, "On Monday I misspelt it on purpose. Only three of you got it right in the test, but nobody said so out loud." Zubin grinned sheepishly. Bhupen went red. He had known, and still he'd said yes.

qa.q: How did the teacher write the word on the board?
qa.a: The teacher wrote "recieve" on the board.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling on Wednesday during the test?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a knot of worry, doubting his own knowledge because the whole class had said the wrong spelling was right.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next time he disagrees with the class?
qa.a: Bhupen could say "I think it's ei" out loud, trusting what he knows even if the group says otherwise.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when the teacher revealed the trick?
qa.a: Zubin looked sheepish, perhaps embarrassed at how easily he'd shouted yes with everyone.

grounding: Over a week, a child follows the class in accepting a misspelling he knows is wrong, worried about standing out, then learns he was right.

passage:
Jahnavi mol, come, sit with your Appachan. You asked why I always tell you to say what you see? I'll tell you. My name is Thomas, and when I was nine, in the little school by the paddy fields, our teacher drew three lines on the blackboard.
"Which is longest?" he asked. I could see it was the first one. Plain as day.
But the boy in front said, "The second." Then the next boy, and the next. Ten boys. All "the second."
My turn came. My ears were burning. I didn't want them to laugh at me.
"The second," I said.
The teacher measured with his ruler. The first one was longest. Everyone laughed at all of us, and I felt like a fool twice over.

qa.q: How many lines did the teacher draw on the blackboard?
qa.a: He drew three lines on the blackboard.

qa.q: Why did young Thomas say "the second" when he could see the first was longest?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at if he disagreed with ten boys, so he went along even though he saw the truth.

qa.q: What choice could young Thomas have made when his turn came?
qa.a: He could have said "the first" quietly and calmly, trusting his own eyes even if the others laughed.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the ten boys all saying the second line?
qa.a: The teacher may have been surprised and a little amused, noticing that the boys followed each other instead of looking for themselves.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a child following a group's wrong answer about which line is longest, afraid of being laughed at even though the truth was visible.

passage:
The quiz master held up the buzzer. "Ten seconds! Which weighs more: a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?"
Tejas knew. They weighed the same. A kilo was a kilo. His father had shown him that once with the kitchen scale.
But Ishita's whole table shouted, "Iron!" The next table shouted, "Iron!" Three seconds left. Everyone was looking at Tejas's table.
His partner whispered, "Iron, iron, just say iron."
Tejas's mouth was dry. If he said "same," and he was wrong, the whole hall would laugh.
"Iron," he said.
"Wrong!" said the quiz master. "They weigh the same."
Tejas stared at the table. He had known.

qa.q: How many seconds did the quiz master give?
qa.a: He gave ten seconds.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about when his mouth went dry?
qa.a: He was worried that if he said "same" and was wrong, the whole hall would laugh at him.

qa.q: What could Tejas remind himself of next time the whole room gives one answer?
qa.a: He could remember the kitchen scale and trust what he knows, since the crowd can be wrong.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas's partner had whispered "same"?
qa.a: With one person agreeing, Tejas would probably have found the courage to give the right answer.

grounding: Shows a child in a timed quiz going along with everyone's wrong answer though he knew the truth, afraid of being laughed at.

passage:
In Class 4 at the Chennai school, the teacher showed two pictures of the same lane. "Which picture has more birds? Hands up!"
Tushar counted. The left had five crows on the wire. The right had seven, two hiding on a roof.
"Left!" said Mahima, and her hand shot up. Then almost every hand followed. "Left! Left!"
Tushar's hand hovered. Last week Mahima's friends had laughed for a whole day when someone said "wrong" in maths. He looked at the roof again. Seven.
Slowly, he raised his hand with everyone else. "Left."
"Let's count," said the teacher. "Right has seven."
Tushar pushed his hand into his pocket. His cheeks were hot.

qa.q: How many crows did the left picture have on the wire?
qa.a: The left had five crows on the wire.

qa.q: Why did Tushar raise his hand for the left picture?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at, as Mahima's friends had done last week, so he followed the group even though he counted seven on the right.

qa.q: How could the teacher help children like Tushar speak up?
qa.a: The teacher could ask children to write their answer before hands go up, so each child answers from their own counting.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima when the teacher counts seven on the right?
qa.a: Mahima may feel embarrassed and surprised, having answered quickly and led the others to the wrong picture.

grounding: Shows a child who counted correctly raising his hand with the group's wrong answer because disagreeing alone felt risky.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof all through the July maths period. "Which jar holds more buttons?" Miss asked. "Hands up for the tall jar." Nearly every hand in the room shot up. Zeenat stared at the short, wide jar. It looked fuller to her. "Zeenat?" Gargi nudged her. "Everybody's saying tall. Just say tall." "But the fat one has more, I think." "If you're wrong, the back bench will laugh at you all week." Zeenat's hand crept up slowly. "Tall," she mumbled. Miss tipped both jars onto the desk and counted aloud. The wide jar won by nine buttons. Gargi gave a small, nervous giggle. "You knew," she whispered. "Why didn't you say?" Zeenat pulled her sleeve over her fingers. "Because everybody else said tall."

qa.q: Which jar did nearly every hand go up for?
qa.a: Nearly every hand shot up for the tall jar.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she mumbled "Tall"?
qa.a: She felt anxious and small; she believed the wide jar was fuller but was scared the back bench would laugh at her all week if she stood alone and was wrong.

qa.q: What small step could help Zeenat say what she really sees next time?
qa.a: She could give her answer with a reason, like "the wide one looks fuller", and remind herself that being wrong in class is normal and quickly forgotten.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel once the buttons were counted?
qa.a: Gargi's nervous giggle and "Why didn't you say?" suggest she felt awkward, noticing that her push to follow everyone kept Zeenat from giving the right answer.

grounding: Illustrates a child giving the group's answer against what she can see because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage: It was the week before Holi, and our classroom smelled of the gulal someone had sneaked in. Ma'am held up two paint pots. "If I mix blue and yellow, what do I get?" Maria answered first and loudly. "Purple!" Then the whole row said purple, and the next row too. I knew it was green. I had mixed them in my drawing book a hundred times. But my mouth said "purple" with everyone else. My ears went hot. Ma'am mixed them on a plate. It turned green, of course. Maria laughed and said, "Oops." Nobody laughed at her. I think about that a lot. I, Divyansh, the boy who knew, stayed quiet for nothing.

qa.q: What colour did Maria shout first?
qa.a: Maria answered first and loudly: "Purple!"

qa.q: Why did Divyansh's ears go hot when he said "purple"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, because he knew from his drawing book that blue and yellow make green but went along with the class anyway.

qa.q: What could Divyansh try the next time the class answers together?
qa.a: He could trust what he has tested himself and say "I think it's green, I've mixed it before", even if he is the only one.

qa.q: What would change if Divyansh had said "green" first?
qa.a: Others who also knew might have joined him, and Maria's loud first answer would not have carried the whole class.

grounding: Shows a child copying the class's wrong answer despite seeing the truth, and the risk of disagreeing alone.

passage: Class 3 note, Christmas week. During the paper-star activity I asked, "Which clock shows half past three?" and held up two cardboard clocks. Tarun wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct. Then he looked around. Most children were writing B, and Dilnaz was already giggling at a friend's slate. Tarun rubbed out his A with his thumb and wrote B. When I asked him later, he said quietly, "I thought A. But everyone put B, and I didn't want them to laugh." What I did next: I praised him for his first answer, privately. The next day I asked the class to answer on slates turned face-down and reveal together, so nobody could copy the crowd.

qa.q: What did Tarun write on his slate at first?
qa.a: He wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct.

qa.q: What made Tarun rub out his answer, and what was he worried about?
qa.a: He saw most children writing B and Dilnaz giggling, and he felt nervous that they would laugh at him for being different.

qa.q: Which choice by the note-writer worked, and why?
qa.a: Having slates turned face-down and revealed together worked, because children answer before they can see and copy the crowd.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's giggling look from Tarun's side?
qa.a: To Tarun it may have looked like proof that anyone who differs gets laughed at, even if Dilnaz was only laughing with a friend.

grounding: Illustrates a young child switching to the majority answer out of fear of being laughed at even though his first answer was right.

passage:
Summer camp, Day 3
Today in the quiz game, Didi drew two lines on the board and asked which one was longer, A or B. I could SEE it was B. It was so obviously B. But Kavitha said A, then the next kid said A, and then everyone said A, even the big ones. When it was my turn my face got hot. I thought, if I say B they'll all laugh, like they laughed at Tarun yesterday. So I said A. Then Didi measured both lines with a ruler. B was longer. Everyone groaned, and Kavitha whispered, "I knew it was B!" So why didn't she say it? Why didn't I?
Wasim

qa.q: Which line was actually longer?
qa.a: B was longer.

qa.q: Why did Wasim say A even though B looked longer?
qa.a: Wasim felt anxious and embarrassed, worried that everyone would laugh the way they had laughed at Tarun.

qa.q: What could Wasim try the next time a group agrees on something that looks wrong?
qa.a: Wasim could say calmly "I think it's B", perhaps adding "I might be wrong", since even Kavitha secretly agreed 🙂.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had said B first?
qa.a: Others, including Wasim, would probably have felt safe to say B too, because one person going first makes disagreeing much easier.

grounding: A child sees everyone pick an answer that looks wrong and goes along, afraid of being laughed at.
